briefdescription.para: The condition of the moment matrix, scaled to a unit diagonal: the estimate of the condition number in the 1-norm, $ \kappa_1(\boldsymbol{D} \boldsymbol{M} \boldsymbol{D}) $ with $ D_{kk} = M_{kk}^{-1/2} $, from a Cholesky (LDLT) factorization of the scaled matrix and its reciprocal condition estimate.

detaileddescription.para:
The monomials of $ \boldsymbol{H} $ carry the unit of length to their degree, so the condition of $ \boldsymbol{M} $ itself would depend on the unit; scaling to a unit diagonal removes this, and a constant factor of the kernels. In the 2-norm, the scaling to a unit diagonal gives a condition within a factor of the basis size $ \binom{d+n}{d} $ of the best diagonal scaling (van der Sluis); the 1-norm condition differs from the 2-norm one by at most that factor as well. For the small, symmetric moment matrices the factorization costs less than the QR factorization of the evaluation.
M

$ \kappa_1 \ge 1 $; infinite for a singular matrix (a pivot of the scaled matrix at the rounding level) or a zero entry on its diagonal.

briefdescription.para: Reproducing kernel (RK) approximation with explicit (direct) shape function gradients.

detaileddescription.para: The shape function of node $ A $ is the kernel $ \phi_A $ (KernelFunction) multiplied by a correction function, \[ \Psi_A(\boldsymbol{x}) = \boldsymbol{H}^T(\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{x}_A)\, \boldsymbol{b}(\boldsymbol{x})\, \phi_A(\boldsymbol{x}), \] where $ \boldsymbol{H} $ is the vector of all monomials up to the completeness order $ n $ (Math::MonomialBasis, first entry $ 1 $) evaluated at the shifted coordinates $ \boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{x}_A $. The coefficient vector $ \boldsymbol{b} $ solves \[ \boldsymbol{M}(\boldsymbol{x})\, \boldsymbol{b}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \boldsymbol{H}_0, \qquad \boldsymbol{M}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \sum_{B} \boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{x}_B)\, \boldsymbol{H}^T(\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{x}_B)\, \phi_B(\boldsymbol{x}), \qquad \boldsymbol{H}_0 = \boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{0}) = [1, 0, \dots, 0]^T, \] with the moment matrix $ \boldsymbol{M} $ summed over the kernels covering $ \boldsymbol{x} $. This enforces the reproducing conditions $ \sum_A \Psi_A(\boldsymbol{x})\, (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{x}_A)^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} = \delta_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}\boldsymbol{0}} $, or equivalently $ \sum_A \Psi_A(\boldsymbol{x})\, \boldsymbol{x}_A^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} = \boldsymbol{x}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} $, for all multi-indices $ |\boldsymbol{\alpha}| \le n $; in particular, the shape functions form a partition of unity. The continuity of $ \Psi_A $ is that of the kernels.

The gradients are the exact derivatives of $ \Psi_A $ (product rule), \[ \Psi_{A,i} = \left( \boldsymbol{b}_{,i}^T \boldsymbol{H} + \boldsymbol{b}^T \boldsymbol{H}_{,i} \right) \phi_A + \boldsymbol{b}^T \boldsymbol{H}\, \phi_{A,i}, \qquad \boldsymbol{b}_{,i} = -\boldsymbol{M}^{-1} \boldsymbol{M}_{,i}\, \boldsymbol{b}, \qquad \boldsymbol{M}_{,i} = \sum_B \left( \boldsymbol{H}_{,i} \boldsymbol{H}^T + \boldsymbol{H} \boldsymbol{H}_{,i}^T \right) \phi_B + \boldsymbol{H} \boldsymbol{H}^T \phi_{B,i}, \] with $ (\bullet)_{,i} = \partial (\bullet) / \partial x_i $ and $ \boldsymbol{H} $ evaluated at $ \boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{x}_A $ (resp. $ \boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{x}_B $). The linear systems are solved with a column-pivoting Householder QR decomposition of $ \boldsymbol{M} $, which is computed once per evaluation point.

One evaluation, four passes over the kernels. First, every candidate kernel is evaluated once, with its gradient if the gradients of the shape functions are asked for (evaluateKernelFunctions()); the values and gradients are kept in the output arrays, which have one entry per candidate. Second, the basis $ \boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{x}_A) $ of every covering kernel (and its gradient) is evaluated once and kept (evaluateBasisOfKernels()): the moment matrix and the shape functions both need it. Third, $ \boldsymbol{M} $ (and $ \boldsymbol{M}_{,i} $) is assembled (assembleMomentMatrix()); fourth, the shape functions follow, overwriting the kernel values. The moment matrix and the vectors of the basis are of a fixed largest size (BasisVector, MomentMatrix); the bases of the kernels, one column per candidate, are the one allocation of an evaluation.

If fewer kernels cover $ \boldsymbol{x} $ than the basis has entries, $ \boldsymbol{M} $ is singular; the completeness order is then reduced for this evaluation point (getCorrectedCompletenessOrder()).

Limit on the condition of the moment matrix (optional). Enough kernels may cover $ \boldsymbol{x} $ and still leave $ \boldsymbol{M} $ nearly singular: at a point on one side of all covering kernels, each at the edge of its support (e.g. the corner of a strongly stretched particle reaching into a void), the corrected kernels extrapolate and $ \Psi_A $ and its gradients become arbitrarily large. With a limit $ \kappa_\mathrm{max} $ on the condition of $ \boldsymbol{M} $, the completeness order of such a point is lowered one order at a time until the condition is below the limit, down to the order $ 0 $ (Shepard functions, $ \Psi_A = \phi_A / \sum_B \phi_B $, bounded by 1), which is always accepted. The condition is that of the diagonally scaled matrix $ \boldsymbol{D} \boldsymbol{M} \boldsymbol{D} $, $ D_{kk} = M_{kk}^{-1/2} $ (conditionOfMomentMatrix()): the scaling makes it independent of the unit of length and of a constant factor of the kernels. Without a limit (the default, $ \kappa_\mathrm{max} = \infty $) the condition is not computed; with a limit, a point below it is evaluated exactly as without one, and a moment matrix of order $ n \ge 1 $ that is singular is evaluated with a lower order as well (only a point that no kernel covers still throws). The lower order costs the point its polynomial completeness: the shape functions jump where the condition crosses the limit, in space and in time, and a particle integrated with such a point no longer passes the patch test of that order.
See ReproducingKernelApproximationImplicit for the variant with implicit gradients.
